Yet the question of what current architectural approaches, including neuro-symbolic and agentic systems, each assume about legal reasoning has received little attention. We argue that design choices about representing legal knowledge, organizing inference, and constraining inputs and outputs shape how a system handles central features of legal reasoning in ways that correspond, with differing strength, to positions in contested jurisprudential debates. We propose a methodology for identifying these architectural features and apply it to four families of legal AI. We then use debates in legal theory to formulate those features as jurisprudentially significant assumptions about legal reasoning that, taken together, form each architecture's implicit picture of legal reasoning. From this, we conclude (1) that the jurisprudential character of legal AI cannot be fully inferred from functional behavior alone; (2) that the fit between an architecture's jurisprudential assumptions and its legal context of use is a design criterion; and (3) that the large-scale deployment of a single architectural approach across heterogeneous legal contexts may create a structural tension with the jurisprudential pluralism of legal practice.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7666719\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/bf00413849\", \"title\": [\"Identifying implicit assumptions\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00413849\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1982, 4]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/s10817-012-9264-3\", \"title\": [\"Eliciting Implicit Assumptions of Mizar Proofs by Property Omission\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/s10817-012-9264-3\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2012, 11, 6]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6818118\", \"title\": [\"From Implicit to Controlled Canonicalizatio…

Specification and Fast Learning of Desired Behavior
Zhiyuan Zhou∗
UC Berkeley
Shreyas Sundara Raman
Brown University
Henry Sowerby
Brown University
Michael L. Littman
Brown University
Abstract
Reinforcement-learning agents seek to maximize a reward signal through environ-
mental interactions. As humans, our job in the learning process is to design reward
functions to express desired behavior and enable the agent to learn such behavior
swiftly. However, designing good reward functions to induce the desired behav-
ior is generally hard, let alone the question of which rewards make learning fast.
In this work, we introduce a family of a reward structures we call Tiered Reward
that addresses both of these questions. We consider the reward-design problem in
tasks formulated as reaching desirable states and avoiding undesirable states. To
start, we propose a strict partial ordering of the policy space to resolve trade-offs
in behavior preference. We prefer policies that reach the good states faster and
with higher probability while avoiding the bad states longer. Next, we introduce
Tiered Reward, a class of environment-independent reward functions and show it is
guaranteed to induce policies that are Pareto-optimal according to our preference
relation. Finally, we demonstrate that Tiered Reward leads to fast learning with
multiple tabular and deep reinforcement-learning algorithms.
1 Introduction
Reinforcement learning (Sutton & Barto, 1998) (RL) is concerned with the problem of learning
to behave to maximize a reward signal. In biological systems, this reward signal is considered to
be the organism’s motivational system, using pain and pleasure to modulate behavior (Porreca &
Navratilova,2017;Leknes&Tracey,2010;Navratilova&Porreca,2014). Inengineeredsystems, how-
ever, rewards must be selected by the system designer (Nagpal et al., 2020; Dewey, 2014). We view
rewards as a kind of programming language—a specification of the agent’s target behavior (Littman
et al., 2017; Zhou & Li, 2022). As arbiters of behavior correctness in the learning process, humans

See [the reusable kernel contract](kernel.md) for application ownership and the
non-research execution proof, and [installation boundaries](installations.md) for
independent records and runtime lifecycles. These remain inside this repository.

The local [improvement application](improvements.md) uses that same kernel contract
in an explicitly new experiment record. Captured public research informs code
proposals; it does not become writable research authority. Untrusted candidate
code runs only in restricted disposable containers, while the host scores its
outputs. An operator review receipt cannot apply code or grant release authority.

The [autonomous context lane](autonomous-context.md) is a separate WAKE application
policy on the existing per-node native authority. An installed capability permits
one selector-field change, gated by recomputed fixed-task and current-native-state
measurements. Proposal generation, adoption and rollback require no per-change
human review. Metadata events preserve research versions and history; candidate
data cannot replace the evaluator, widen permissions, modify code or create a
competing research store. Native replay owns the policy after restart.

> **Current specification.** This document explains why the present system is shaped this way: its trust boundary, durable record, governance model and known limits. Current local procedures belong in `standalone.md`; public mirror publishing belongs in `cloud.md`. Maintainer navigation, environment checks and reproducible validation guidance belong in `development.md`.

**WAKE✳︎** is infrastructure for continuity of accountable work, not continuity of a model instance. Its stable sequence is **Record → Context → Proposal → Governance → Transition → Receipt**.
